# Citations index

Source: *The Squat* - Starting Strength, reference pages 1-35 (combined PDF pages 4-38).
reference page N = combined PDF page N+3

Every quote below is verbatim from the reference document and was checked against the PDF by hand. A fabricated citation would be worse here than no citation at all.

## By criterion

### Squat depth  
`depth` · ref p. 2, 16, 18, 22, 33 · Fig 2-1, 2-10

**Standard:**

> Correctly is deep, with hips dropping below level with the top of the patellas. Correctly is therefore full range of motion.

**Supporting:**

> The top of the patella (A) and the hip joint, as identified by the apex in the crease of the shorts (B). The B side of the plane formed by these two points must drop below parallel with the ground.

**Feedback drawn from ref p. 18, 33:**

> Any squat that is not deep is a partial squat. If you are high, check that your stance is wide enough but not too wide, that your toes are out enough, and that your knees are tracking parallel to your feet - most people who squat high do not shove their knees out enough.

### Back angle  
`back_angle` · ref p. 9, 11, 23, 32, 35 · Fig 2-5, 2-13, 2-22

**Standard:**

> The back angle is formed by the plane of the torso and the floor, which is assumed to be horizontal (meaning level, perpendicular to the force of gravity).

**Supporting:**

> your back is inclined at about a 45-degree angle, not at all vertical

**Stated failure mode:**

> Your back will (usually) be too vertical, due to a faulty mental picture of what your hips do when you squat or due to the incorrect placement of the bar on your back, or your back will be too horizontal, due to your failure to keep your chest up. Either error will adversely affect hip drive and depth.

**Feedback drawn from ref p. 32, 33:**

> Most people have a picture in their minds of a vertical torso during the squat. The back angle will not be vertical at all; sit back, lean forward, and shove your knees out. Balance problems usually indicate a back angle that is too vertical.

### Bar path over the midfoot  
`bar_path_over_midfoot` · ref p. 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 · Fig 2-5, 2-7

**Standard:**

> So not only is a straight line the shortest distance between two points, but a straight vertical line is also the most efficient bar path for a barbell moving through space in a gravitational framework.

**Supporting:**

> "good technique" in barbell training is easily and understandably defined as the ability of the lifter to keep the bar vertically aligned with the balance point.

**Definition:**

> the midfoot is exactly halfway between either end of the sole of the shoe.

**Feedback drawn from ref p. 11, 12:**

> When the bar is off-balance, the added energy you must expend due to the leverage of the off-balance load makes the weight harder to lift. Keep the bar travelling in a vertical line over the middle of the foot through the complete range of motion.

### Hip drive out of the bottom  
`hip_drive` · ref p. 1, 23, 24, 35 · Fig 2-14

**Standard:**

> come up out of the bottom by driving your butt straight up in the air. Up, not forward.

**Stated failure mode:**

> You will lift your chest instead of driving your hips up. This will kill your power out of the bottom by making your back angle too vertical.

**Feedback drawn from ref p. 24:**

> Think about a chain hooked to your hips, pulling you straight up out of the bottom. Do not think about your knees straightening out, do not think about your feet pushing against the floor. Just drive your hips up out of the bottom.

### Knee position at the bottom (sagittal)  
`knee_forward_of_toes` · ref p. 23 · Fig 2-13

**Standard:**

> the hips are back, the knees are just a little forward of the toes, and the back is at an angle (about 45 degrees) that will place the bar over the middle of the foot.

### Heels flat on the floor  
`heels_flat` · ref p. 23 · Fig 2-13

**Standard:**

> The femurs are parallel to the feet, the feet are flat on the ground at the correct angle

**Supporting:**

> Assume the bottom position with knees out, toes out, and heels down.

### Bar placement on the back  
`bar_placement_low_bar` · ref p. 13, 30, 31, 35 · Fig 2-19

**Standard:**

> The bar should therefore be in the lowest secure position it can occupy on the back, right below the spine of the scapula

**Stated failure mode:**

> You will place the bar too high on your back. This will adversely affect your back angle and your hip drive.

### Eye gaze direction  
`eye_gaze` · ref p. 24, 25, 27, 35 · Fig 2-15, 2-16

**Standard:**

> fix your eyes on a position on the floor 4 or 5 feet in front of you

**Stated failure mode:**

> You will fail to look down. This will kill your hip drive.

### Knees shoved out  
`knees_out` · ref p. 14, 22, 33, 35

**Standard:**

> You will fail to shove your knees out as you start down. This will make correct depth hard to attain and will kill your hip drive.

**Supporting:**

> Most people who have problems with the squat - at this rank novice level as well as later on - do not shove their knees out enough.

### Stance width and toe angle  
`stance` · ref p. 14, 20, 21, 32, 35 · Fig 2-12

**Standard:**

> We will use a fairly neutral foot placement, with the heels about shoulder width apart and the toes pointed out at about 30 degrees.

**Stated failure mode:**

> Your stance will be either too narrow or too wide, with your toes usually pointed too forward. This will result in a squat that is not below parallel.

### Rack height and unracking procedure  
`rack_height` · ref p. 28, 31, 35

**Standard:**

> Set the rack height so that the bar in the rack is at about the level of your mid-sternum.

**Stated failure mode:**

> You will set the bar in the rack in a position that is too high. This will make the preferred position on the back difficult to attain.
